rationale: A wins because it knows where the story stops and where the proof has to start. Its strongest line, "Figma turns designs into shippable React code — moving onto the developers' turf," is testable and paired with the right caveat: show the code or shut up. B has useful raw material, but "Figma just picked a fight with every AI tool that turns a prompt into an app" is the kind of over-caffeinated framing that sounds sharp until a reporter asks which market, which competitors, and whether the product actually does prompt-to-app.
gaps_in_A: "Figma's first move after the Adobe deal died: ship, not sell" overstates the supplied facts. The update says the launch follows the Adobe deal collapse; it does not prove this is the first move or that Figma is answering the failed deal.
"shippable React code" is strong but slightly ahead of the evidence. The update says Make exports React and HTML/CSS; whether it is shippable is exactly what the angle needs to prove.
The first angle could name the design-to-code incumbent context it needs without inventing it. It flags the gap, but the founder would still need competitor proof before pitching category creation.
gaps_in_B: "Figma just picked a fight with every AI tool that turns a prompt into an app" invents the competitive field and overstates the product. The facts support design-to-code export, not a blanket prompt-to-app showdown.
"dominated by smaller AI-native code-generation startups" is outside the update. Maybe true in the market, but this judge is not giving credit for facts smuggled in from model memory.
"The Adobe deal died. Figma's answer was to launch its biggest bet yet" piles motive and magnitude onto a sequence. The update gives chronology, not intent, and definitely not "biggest bet yet."

"what happens to junior front-end developers?" is a plausible reported feature, but the set leans on labor impact the update does not establish. It needs to be framed as a question with heavy proof, not as a launch-cycle certainty.
